title: The Tooth That Kept the Tool Marks — Neanderthal Molar Grooves, Villabruna Caries Scraping, Mehrgarh Bow-Drills & Lonche Beeswax

teenKit.tldr: Prehistoric teeth reveal that humans have been aggressively trying to fix their dental pain for tens of thousands of years using everything from bone toothpicks to flint drills. However, while high-tech tools like scanning electron microscopes can show us *what* physical gestures ancient people made, they can never truly tell us if the treatment cured the patient or just made them suffer more.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It forces us to realize that humans have always looked at pain and panicked into action, proving that the thin line between a brilliant medical breakthrough and a total disaster is as old as humanity itself.
keyTakeaways: Neanderthals and early humans left microscopic tool marks on their teeth, proving prehistoric dental care goes back way farther than modern history books suggest.
Advanced tech like micro-CT scans and FTIR spectroscopy let scientists act like microscopic detectives, reading chemical and physical clues left behind in ancient tooth enamel.
Finding physical evidence of a medical procedure doesn't mean it worked; artifacts show desperate actions, but they rarely tell us if the patient actually survived or healed.

quiz.question: What is the primary limitation when scientists analyze ancient dental tool marks or drilled teeth?
options: The tools used by prehistoric humans are completely untraceable.
Tooth enamel dissolves too quickly to preserve any physical evidence past a few decades.
Physical tool marks show what action was done, but they cannot tell us the patient's intent or if the treatment actually worked.
Micro-CT scans only work on modern teeth, not ancient ones.
